segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus responded by speaking to them again in parables. He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The kingdom of the heavens may be compared to a king who gave a wedding banquet for his son.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He sent his slaves to call those who had been invited to the wedding banquet, but they would not come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Again he sent other slaves, saying, ‘Tell those who have been invited: “Look, I have prepared my dinner; my bulls and fattened cattle have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding banquet.”’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But they paid no attention and went away, one to his own field, another to his business.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The rest seized his slaves, abused them, and killed them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The king was enraged. He sent his troops, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then he said to his slaves, ‘The wedding banquet is ready, but those who were invited were not worthy.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So go to where the roads lead out, and invite to the wedding banquet as many as you find.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So those slaves went out into the roads and gathered everyone they found, both bad and good, and the wedding banquet was filled with guests.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw a man there who was not wearing a wedding garment,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?’ But the man was left speechless.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then the king said to the servants, ‘Bind him hand and foot and throw him out into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For many are invited, but few are chosen.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the Pharisees went and plotted together how to trap him in what he said.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They sent their disciples to him, together with the Herodians, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth. You defer to no one, for you pay no regard to people’s standing.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So tell us what you think: Is it permitted to pay the tax to Caesar or not?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, knowing their malice, said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you testing me, you hypocrites?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Show me the coin used for the tax.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they brought him a denarius.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Caesar’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “So give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this they were amazed, and they left him and went away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That same day Sadducees came to him, saying that there is no resurrection, and they put a question to him:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies without children, his brother shall marry his wife and raise up offspring for his brother.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and since he had no offspring he left his wife to his brother.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The same happened with the second and the third, and so on through all seven.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Last of all, the woman died.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be, of the seven? For they all had her.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels of God in heaven.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead but of the living.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the crowds heard this, they were astounded at his teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the Pharisees heard that he had left the Sadducees speechless, they gathered together.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And one of them, an expert in the law, put a question to him, testing him:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: This is the great and first commandment.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: A second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: On these two commandments the whole Law hangs, and the Prophets.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus put a question to them:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What do you think about the Messiah? Whose son is he?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “David’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet”’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If, then, David calls him Lord, how is he his son?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And no one was able to answer him a word, and from that day on no one dared to put any more questions to him.

notes.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that Matthew uses regularly and that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” The meaning is not in dispute: it is Matthew’s way of speaking of God’s reign.

The Greek word names a person owned by a master, not a hired employee; a king’s household was staffed by such people, some of them of considerable standing. Many English versions soften it to “servants,” though several recent ones use “slaves.” The attendants in verse 13 are a different Greek word and are rendered “servants.”

notes.traditional: called (“many are called, but few are chosen”)
notes.note: The word is from the same root as the verb used throughout the parable for inviting the guests (verses 3, 4, 8 and 9), so “invited” keeps the closing saying tied to the story it sums up. The traditional “called” is equally accurate, and it is the usual rendering of this word in the letters. Some recent versions also have “invited” here.

The Herodians are mentioned only in the Gospels, and their exact identity is uncertain; the name suggests supporters of the Herodian dynasty, whose rule depended on Rome. Their presence alongside the Pharisees’ disciples sharpens the trap: refusing the tax could be reported as sedition, while endorsing it would offend popular feeling.

The Greek borrows the Latin word census and refers to the head tax Rome levied on its provincial subjects. It was widely resented in Judea as a mark of foreign rule. It was paid in Roman coin, and the denarius of the period typically bore the emperor’s portrait and an inscription naming him as son of the deified Augustus, which is the point of Jesus’ question in verse 20.

The verb means to put someone to the test, here with the aim of trapping him. Older versions have “tempt,” which in modern English suggests enticement to sin; most recent translations use “test” in this passage, as here and in verse 35.

The questioners asked whether it is permitted to “give” the tax; Jesus answers with a stronger verb that commonly means to pay what is owed or return what belongs to someone. “Render” carries this but is now archaic. The implication that the coin already belongs to Caesar, and that something else belongs to God, is generally recognized.

notes.phrase: saying that there is no resurrection
notes.traditional: who say there is no resurrection
notes.note: In the Greek text followed here the phrase has no article, so it most naturally means the Sadducees came asserting that there is no resurrection. Many manuscripts add the article, giving “who say there is no resurrection,” a general description of the group like that in Mark and Luke; many translations render it that way. Either way, denial of resurrection was a known Sadducean position.

notes.phrase: his brother shall marry his wife
notes.note: The Sadducees paraphrase the law of levirate marriage in Deuteronomy 25:5, with wording that also echoes Genesis 38:8. Under it a dead man’s brother married the widow, and the first son was counted as the dead man’s heir. The Greek verb is a technical one for marrying as a brother-in-law.

Manuscripts differ here: some read “angels of God,” others simply “angels.” The edition translated here includes “of God”; other critical editions and many modern translations omit it. The sense is unaffected.

The word names a man learned in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with those elsewhere called scribes. “Lawyer,” kept by many versions, now suggests an attorney who represents clients in court. Several modern translations use “expert in the law” or something close to it.

The Greek word translates the Hebrew for “anointed one” and is here a title, the expected king of David’s line, not a name for Jesus. “Messiah” lets the modern reader hear a title, as the Pharisees did. Several modern translations make the same choice in passages like this and keep “Christ” where it functions as a name.

notes.phrase: The Lord said to my Lord
notes.note: The quotation is Psalm 110:1. In Hebrew the first “Lord” is the divine name and the second is a different word for a master or king; the Greek uses the same word for both. Jesus’ argument rests on premises his hearers shared: that David is the speaker and that the one he addresses is the Messiah, so that David calls his own descendant his superior.

With καλέω it means both “invite” (banquet parables) and “call” (Paul’s vocabulary of calling), so a rule is needed for when the link to invitation is shown and when “called” is kept.
